title: Replicant Data — November 4, 2026
lead: Research on physical calibration, robot learning, multi-machine planning and communication standards.

news.title: A robot calibrates a physical simulator by choosing its own experiments
news.summary: Researchers introduced CUE, which tests physical interactions and updates the physics in a simulated scene. In billiards experiments they report a 72 percent reduction in ball-position prediction error across 25 simulated settings with hidden physical properties.
news.details: Given a high-level instruction, CUE observes the surroundings, proposes parameters for its physical simulation and predicts how objects will move. It then compares the prediction with the observed result and selects the next experiment where the model is least accurate. This is active calibration: the machine takes measurements through action instead of fitting everything from an existing fixed dataset. The paper describes a real-to-simulation-to-real loop in which the system can proceed without a human manually resetting the scene after each test.

Billiard collisions provide an observable benchmark, but only a narrow range of friction and restitution behavior.

news.body:
A picture of a pool table shows where the balls are but not how quickly they will slow down on the felt. A robot planning its next move needs to estimate friction and how much speed remains after a collision. Researchers led by Xilun Zhang and Marco Pavone presented CUE on November 2, short for Calibration Using Exploration. Rather than merely watch recordings, the system chooses real interactions that reveal physical properties missing from its virtual representation of the scene.

Given a high-level instruction, CUE observes the surroundings, proposes parameters for its physical simulation and predicts how objects will move. It then compares the prediction with the observed result and selects the next experiment where the model is least accurate. This is active calibration: the machine takes measurements through action instead of fitting everything from an existing fixed dataset. The paper describes a real-to-simulation-to-real loop in which the system can proceed without a human manually resetting the scene after each test.

Across 25 simulated hidden-physics conditions, the authors report reducing held-out billiard-ball position error by 72 percent against the strongest baseline. They also describe an experiment on a real pool table. This figure concerns prediction error for the tested dynamics; it is not a success rate for arbitrary robotic work. The paper does not establish an equivalent improvement for cloth, irregular packaging or complicated household objects. The evidence is an author-reported experimental study rather than independent replication.

The distinctive component is experiment selection driven by discrepancy between predicted and observed dynamics, rather than parameter fitting on a fixed collection of trajectories. A meaningful reproduction would separate perception error, contact modeling and physical parameter identification. Billiard collisions provide an observable benchmark, but only a narrow range of friction and restitution behavior.

news.title: A sub-$2,500 open tabletop arena for competing robots
news.summary: ETH Zurich researchers released KlaskTron, a tabletop system in which two robotic mechanisms learn competitive play. The authors estimate hardware at under 2,500 US dollars and report transferring simulated control to the physical apparatus without additional training.
news.details: Both mechanisms use CoreXY gantry arrangements and brushless motors. The team built a digital twin in NVIDIA Isaac Lab, a simulation environment used in robot development, and trained a model of how the motors respond to commands. They report transferring the resulting control policy from simulation to the real tabletop setup without further on-hardware training. Hardware drawings, a bill of materials, assembly instructions, control code and experiment configurations are publicly available. These resources make it possible for other laboratories to scrutinize more than a demonstration video.
news.technical_novelty: Both mechanisms use CoreXY gantry arrangements and brushless motors. The team built a digital twin in NVIDIA Isaac Lab, a simulation environment used in robot development, and trained a model of how the motors respond to commands. They report transferring the resulting control policy from simulation to the real tabletop setup without further on-hardware training. Hardware drawings, a bill of materials, assembly instructions, control code and experiment configurations are publicly available. These resources make it possible for other laboratories to scrutinize more than a demonstration video.
news.engineering_impact: Reproducibility rests on unusually concrete artifacts: mechanical drawings, parts lists, an actuator model and the reinforcement-learning code. Testing another build should record controller latency, backlash and calibration drift rather than assume the systems are identical. The competitive setup provides continually changing conditions for examining policy stability.
news.limitations: Competition differs from following a fixed movement script because the opponent changes the conditions at every turn. The authors observed behaviors responding to an adversary, but the paper does not guarantee stable play on any independently assembled copy. Precise construction and actuator calibration still matter. Nor does success on a tabletop establish that large humanoids can coordinate safely among people. The practical research contribution is a relatively affordable physical platform on which claims about policy transfer and interaction can be tested.
news.evidence_status: Evidence: results and limitations are reported by the study authors; independent replication has not been established.
news.body:
Studying how two learning machines respond to each other is difficult when experiments depend on expensive full-size robots. ETH Zurich researchers proposed a smaller alternative: KlaskTron, a tabletop testbed inspired by the game KLASK. Two controlled mechanisms compete across a board and must respond to the other side's changing actions. The paper appeared on November 2, with the researchers estimating component cost below 2,500 US dollars. The system is primarily a repeatable environment for experiments in multi-agent robot learning, not a product announcement for a commercial arcade game.

Both mechanisms use CoreXY gantry arrangements and brushless motors. The team built a digital twin in NVIDIA Isaac Lab, a simulation environment used in robot development, and trained a model of how the motors respond to commands. They report transferring the resulting control policy from simulation to the real tabletop setup without further on-hardware training. Hardware drawings, a bill of materials, assembly instructions, control code and experiment configurations are publicly available. These resources make it possible for other laboratories to scrutinize more than a demonstration video.

Competition differs from following a fixed movement script because the opponent changes the conditions at every turn. The authors observed behaviors responding to an adversary, but the paper does not guarantee stable play on any independently assembled copy. Precise construction and actuator calibration still matter. Nor does success on a tabletop establish that large humanoids can coordinate safely among people. The practical research contribution is a relatively affordable physical platform on which claims about policy transfer and interaction can be tested.

Reproducibility rests on unusually concrete artifacts: mechanical drawings, parts lists, an actuator model and the reinforcement-learning code. Testing another build should record controller latency, backlash and calibration drift rather than assume the systems are identical. The competitive setup provides continually changing conditions for examining policy stability.

news.title: Coding agents boost simulated warehouse throughput by 22–60 percent
news.summary: Researchers at the University of Southern California, UC Irvine and Symbotic let language-model agents modify a multi-robot warehouse planner. Six simulation campaigns increased throughput by 22 to 60 percent, although some changes raised planning computation more than one hundredfold.
news.details: The original planner assigned work to multiple machines while choosing routes that avoid conflicts. Coding agents proposed program changes, simulated the resulting traffic and measured whether more jobs could be completed. Each improvement was preserved as a sequence of scored source-code patches rather than a single opaque model output. Six independent tuning campaigns were evaluated, including tests with different starting conditions, fleet sizes and warehouse configurations. That makes it possible to inspect what changed, but it does not mean every change will work in a new industrial environment.
news.technical_novelty: The original planner assigned work to multiple machines while choosing routes that avoid conflicts. Coding agents proposed program changes, simulated the resulting traffic and measured whether more jobs could be completed. Each improvement was preserved as a sequence of scored source-code patches rather than a single opaque model output. Six independent tuning campaigns were evaluated, including tests with different starting conditions, fleet sizes and warehouse configurations. That makes it possible to inspect what changed, but it does not mean every change will work in a new industrial environment.
news.engineering_impact: The agents produced a chain of scored, reviewable commits rather than a single untraceable rewrite. Reproduction would require matching random seeds, checking conflict resolution and profiling processor use as carefully as throughput. A policy that delivers the highest simulated flow may be unusable if its computation exceeds the control loop's timing budget.
news.limitations: Across the six campaigns, simulated throughput improved by 22 to 60 percent. Some gains survived a different layout or larger fleet but shrank for smaller fleets and nearly disappeared with an outbound-heavy workload. Final modifications ran to roughly 700–2,400 lines of code, while some versions multiplied planning compute by more than one hundred. These figures do not measure output from a live customer warehouse and do not include the cost of additional hardware. Successful optimization of one benchmark is not a substitute for safety review and software testing.
news.evidence_status: Evidence: results and limitations are reported by the study authors; independent replication has not been established.
news.organization: University of Southern California, UC Irvine and Symbotic
news.body:
Even when warehouse robots know which jobs they should do, they can block one another in narrow corridors or at crowded crossings. Researchers from the University of Southern California, UC Irvine and Symbotic investigated an unusual use of language models: improving the source code of an existing warehouse traffic planner instead of replacing the robots' controllers. Their paper, Late Autumn, appeared on November 2. The experiments used a simulated automated warehouse modeled on an existing facility, with attention to problems that arise from its particular layout.

The original planner assigned work to multiple machines while choosing routes that avoid conflicts. Coding agents proposed program changes, simulated the resulting traffic and measured whether more jobs could be completed. Each improvement was preserved as a sequence of scored source-code patches rather than a single opaque model output. Six independent tuning campaigns were evaluated, including tests with different starting conditions, fleet sizes and warehouse configurations. That makes it possible to inspect what changed, but it does not mean every change will work in a new industrial environment.

Across the six campaigns, simulated throughput improved by 22 to 60 percent. Some gains survived a different layout or larger fleet but shrank for smaller fleets and nearly disappeared with an outbound-heavy workload. Final modifications ran to roughly 700–2,400 lines of code, while some versions multiplied planning compute by more than one hundred. These figures do not measure output from a live customer warehouse and do not include the cost of additional hardware. Successful optimization of one benchmark is not a substitute for safety review and software testing.

The agents produced a chain of scored, reviewable commits rather than a single untraceable rewrite. Reproduction would require matching random seeds, checking conflict resolution and profiling processor use as carefully as throughput. A policy that delivers the highest simulated flow may be unusable if its computation exceeds the control loop's timing budget.

news.title: A humanoid chains walking and handling skills learned separately
news.summary: Seoul National University researchers introduced RISE, a framework linking separately recorded examples of locomotion and object handling. They report 87.3 percent mean success in simulation and a 20-percentage-point advantage over a baseline in experiments with a real Unitree G1.
news.details: The architecture shares visual and language processing across several action specialists, with a coordinator deciding which behavior should be active. During training a specialist receives greater responsibility for examples it predicts accurately. Changes in responsibility weights then help signal a transition to another phase of the task. The real robot is a Unitree G1 fitted with two dexterous hands and 43 controllable degrees of freedom. That is an impressive physical configuration, but it does not mean the model can invent arbitrary skills beyond the kinds of demonstrations used for learning.
news.technical_novelty: The architecture shares visual and language processing across several action specialists, with a coordinator deciding which behavior should be active. During training a specialist receives greater responsibility for examples it predicts accurately. Changes in responsibility weights then help signal a transition to another phase of the task. The real robot is a Unitree G1 fitted with two dexterous hands and 43 controllable degrees of freedom. That is an impressive physical configuration, but it does not mean the model can invent arbitrary skills beyond the kinds of demonstrations used for learning.
news.engineering_impact: The design question is how specialist weights identify skill boundaries without additional labeled transition demonstrations. Reproduction should separate the failure rates of individual policies from errors in deciding when to switch. The two-to-four-stage simulation figures must not be treated as interchangeable with the real robot's longer sequences.
news.limitations: For simulated tasks comprising two to four stages, the team reports an 87.3 percent mean success rate against 73.6 percent for its single-expert comparison. On a real G1, the researchers report a 20-percentage-point advantage, with sequences of up to five stages. The university explicitly identifies truly simultaneous locomotion and dexterous manipulation as future work. Watching a robot walk to a table, pick up an object and move again is evidence of sequential skill composition, not proof of unrestricted autonomy in a crowded home.
news.evidence_status: Evidence: performance figures are reported by the university on behalf of the research team; independent replication is not established.
news.body:
A humanoid robot that can walk and a robot that can grasp a bottle do not automatically know when to switch between those two activities. On October 30, Seoul National University described RISE, developed by Professor Songhwai Oh's team. The name means Responsibility-Induced Specialized Experts, referring to several action models that develop distinct roles during training. The system uses independently collected walking and manipulation demonstrations instead of requiring a recording of every complete sequence. The paper was accepted at the IROS 2026 robotics conference.

The architecture shares visual and language processing across several action specialists, with a coordinator deciding which behavior should be active. During training a specialist receives greater responsibility for examples it predicts accurately. Changes in responsibility weights then help signal a transition to another phase of the task. The real robot is a Unitree G1 fitted with two dexterous hands and 43 controllable degrees of freedom. That is an impressive physical configuration, but it does not mean the model can invent arbitrary skills beyond the kinds of demonstrations used for learning.

For simulated tasks comprising two to four stages, the team reports an 87.3 percent mean success rate against 73.6 percent for its single-expert comparison. On a real G1, the researchers report a 20-percentage-point advantage, with sequences of up to five stages. The university explicitly identifies truly simultaneous locomotion and dexterous manipulation as future work. Watching a robot walk to a table, pick up an object and move again is evidence of sequential skill composition, not proof of unrestricted autonomy in a crowded home.

The design question is how specialist weights identify skill boundaries without additional labeled transition demonstrations. Reproduction should separate the failure rates of individual policies from errors in deciding when to switch. The two-to-four-stage simulation figures must not be treated as interchangeable with the real robot's longer sequences.

news.title: Communication compatibility is not the same as robot navigation or safety
news.summary: The Association for Advancing Automation explained ISO 21423:2026 on November 2 as a communications framework for industrial mobile robots from different vendors. The actual standard was published on October 14 and excludes requirements for safety and navigation.
news.details: The scope covers communications among industrial mobile robots, fleet-management programs and other devices in the shared workplace, including automated doors and lifts. The industry group describes information about location, speed, direction, tasks and equipment availability as relevant exchanges. A common message convention can reduce the need for one-off connections between different suppliers. However, sharing state does not calculate collision-free routes, decide who has priority in a corridor or replace an emergency-stop system. Interoperability at the data layer must be distinguished from coordinated physical behavior.
news.technical_novelty: The scope covers communications among industrial mobile robots, fleet-management programs and other devices in the shared workplace, including automated doors and lifts. The industry group describes information about location, speed, direction, tasks and equipment availability as relevant exchanges. A common message convention can reduce the need for one-off connections between different suppliers. However, sharing state does not calculate collision-free routes, decide who has priority in a corridor or replace an emergency-stop system. Interoperability at the data layer must be distinguished from coordinated physical behavior.
news.engineering_impact: A technical specification must distinguish reported state, issued commands and the fleet manager's authority. Procurement and conformance checks need the primary standard text rather than relying exclusively on a trade association summary. Because safety is outside scope, failure-mode analysis and protective controls remain separate engineering obligations.
news.limitations: The ISO catalogue explicitly states that the document contains no safety requirements and no navigation requirements. Consumer, military, medical and public-road applications are also excluded. A claim of compliance therefore cannot be treated as permission to deploy a mixed fleet without site-specific testing. Engineers still need to verify the actual interfaces, building integrations and responses to lost communication. A standard can define a shared language for equipment while leaving the most difficult motion and safety problems to the systems built around it.
news.evidence_status: Evidence: an industry explanation refers to the formal standard; it is not an equipment validation study.
news.body:
A large warehouse can operate mobile robots from multiple vendors, yet their fleet managers may disagree about how to describe a machine's position, assignment or state. On November 2 the Association for Advancing Automation discussed ISO 21423:2026, a communications and interoperability standard for industrial mobile robots. The International Organization for Standardization had actually published the document on October 14. The November announcement is an explanation of the existing standard, not the launch of a newly invented navigation system.

The scope covers communications among industrial mobile robots, fleet-management programs and other devices in the shared workplace, including automated doors and lifts. The industry group describes information about location, speed, direction, tasks and equipment availability as relevant exchanges. A common message convention can reduce the need for one-off connections between different suppliers. However, sharing state does not calculate collision-free routes, decide who has priority in a corridor or replace an emergency-stop system. Interoperability at the data layer must be distinguished from coordinated physical behavior.

The ISO catalogue explicitly states that the document contains no safety requirements and no navigation requirements. Consumer, military, medical and public-road applications are also excluded. A claim of compliance therefore cannot be treated as permission to deploy a mixed fleet without site-specific testing. Engineers still need to verify the actual interfaces, building integrations and responses to lost communication. A standard can define a shared language for equipment while leaving the most difficult motion and safety problems to the systems built around it.

A technical specification must distinguish reported state, issued commands and the fleet manager's authority. Procurement and conformance checks need the primary standard text rather than relying exclusively on a trade association summary. Because safety is outside scope, failure-mode analysis and protective controls remain separate engineering obligations.
